prompt: A database keeps one copy of its data, on one machine. What does the CAP theorem say it has to give up?
hint: The theorem is about copies joined by a network.

choices.text: Nothing: with one copy there is no partition to choose under
choices.why: Right. A single copy is consistent and available until the machine dies; the choice appears with the second copy.

choices.text: Partition tolerance, since it has no network to survive
choices.why: That reads P as a feature to pick. With one copy there is simply nothing to partition.

choices.text: Availability, because one machine is a single point of failure
choices.why: A crash is not what the theorem's A is about: it speaks of nodes that have not failed.

choices.text: Consistency, because nothing checks the one copy against another
choices.why: One copy cannot disagree with itself; every read sees the last write.

prompt: Why is "pick two of consistency, availability and partition tolerance" a misleading summary?

choices.text: Because consistency and availability can both be kept if replication is fast enough
choices.why: Speed does not help a copy that cannot hear the other at all.

choices.text: Because partitions happen whether you choose them or not
choices.why: Right. P is not on the menu; the choice is what each copy does while one is happening.

choices.text: Because the theorem was never proved, only conjectured
choices.why: Gilbert and Lynch proved it in 2002.

choices.text: Because modern databases offer all three at once
choices.why: No system can, during a partition; that is what the proof shows.

prompt: In the theorem, what does consistency promise?
hint: It is not the C of ACID.

choices.text: Every transaction leaves the schema's rules intact
choices.why: That is the C in ACID, a different promise.

choices.text: Once a write is acknowledged, no read anywhere returns the value from before it
choices.why: Right: linearisability, as if there were one copy.

choices.text: All copies end up agreeing with each other eventually, once the writes stop coming in
choices.why: That is eventual consistency, which is much weaker.

choices.text: The data is stored in the same format on every node
choices.why: Format has nothing to do with it; the promise is about what a read can see.

prompt: During a partition the São Paulo copy keeps selling and Lisbon refuses every sale until the link returns. What has the system chosen?
hint: Ask what each copy does with a request it cannot confirm.

choices.text: Consistency, because Lisbon refused
choices.why: São Paulo answered without knowing about Lisbon, so a stale or double sale is possible.

choices.text: Availability, because São Paulo sold
choices.why: Lisbon refused requests while its node was alive, so it is not available in the proof's sense.

choices.text: Neither guarantee, in the theorem's sense
choices.why: Right. One copy answers without knowing the latest write and the other refuses: it pays both costs.

choices.text: Both, since each city got one of them
choices.why: A guarantee about the system has to hold everywhere, not in one city each.

prompt: Match each word of the theorem to what it means there.
hint: One description belongs to none of them.

pairs.right: a read never returns a value older than an acknowledged write
every node that has not failed answers, without an error
the network between copies loses messages

prompt: Two copies are 4,000 km apart, joined by fibre where light covers about 200,000 km a second. What is the shortest a write that waits for the far copy's acknowledgement can take, in milliseconds?
What does the "ELC" half of PACELC describe?

choices.text: The choice between latency and consistency while the network works
choices.why: Right: Else, Latency or Consistency. It is the cost paid on ordinary days.

choices.text: What happens when a node runs out of memory
choices.why: PACELC is about copies agreeing, not about resources.

choices.text: The choice between availability and consistency during a partition
choices.why: That is the PAC half, which is CAP itself.

choices.text: How to elect a new leader once the old one is gone
choices.why: Elections are a mechanism lesson 9 shows; the letters name a trade-off.

prompt: A system answers writes as soon as one copy has them. On the developer's laptop every copy runs on the same machine. Why does a bug about stale reads not show up there?
hint: How long is the window between the answer and the other copies having it?

choices.text: Because a laptop runs every copy in one process, which turns replication off entirely
choices.why: Replication still runs; it just finishes very fast.

choices.text: Because the replication window is too short to hit when copies share one machine
choices.why: Right. The window exists, but it is far smaller than the time between two requests a developer types.

choices.text: Because stale reads need a partition, and a laptop has no network
choices.why: Under EL a stale read needs no partition at all, only a read that lands before replication finishes.

choices.text: Because the bug lives in the driver, and the driver is configured differently in production
choices.why: Nothing in the scenario changes the driver; the difference is the distance between copies.

prompt: A system that refuses during a partition and waits for its copies the rest of the time is classified as PC/___.
Which of the shop's operations should give up availability before it gives up consistency?
hint: Ask what a disagreement between copies costs.

choices.text: Counting a page view
choices.why: A count a few views behind harms nobody; a failed page does.

choices.text: Showing "customers also bought"
choices.why: Slightly old suggestions are fine; an empty box is worse.

choices.text: Taking the last unit out of stock
choices.why: Right. Two copies that disagree sell it twice, and that is a refund and an apology.

choices.text: Adding an item to a basket
choices.why: A basket a second behind is harmless; a basket that refuses stops the sale.

prompt: Out of the box, a MongoDB replica set acknowledges a write when…

choices.text: the primary alone has it
choices.why: That was the default before MongoDB 5.0; it is now a majority.

choices.text: every member has it
choices.why: One slow member would then hold up every write.

choices.text: a majority of the members have it
choices.why: Right: the implicit default write concern is majority.

choices.text: the client chooses, and there is no default
choices.why: The client can choose, and there is a default when it does not.

prompt: A team moves page-view counting from their strict database to a store that answers at once and replicates later. What did they buy, and what did they pay?
hint: Use the two costs the section names.

choices.text: They bought lower latency on every request and paid with counts that lag a little
choices.why: Right. A count that lags harms nobody, and the old cost was paid on every view.

choices.text: They bought consistency and paid with availability
choices.why: It is the reverse: the new store answers without waiting for copies.

choices.text: They bought nothing, since the theorem only applies during partitions
choices.why: The latency cost is paid on ordinary days; that is PACELC's point.

choices.text: They bought durability and paid with speed
choices.why: Durability is not the trade here, and the move made things faster.

prompt: A shop charges a card twice because two copies of a payment record disagreed for a moment. When is a failure like this usually found?

choices.text: At once, because the database raises an error
choices.why: Nothing errors: each copy did what it was configured to do.

choices.text: In the developer's tests, before release
choices.why: On one machine the window is too short to hit.

choices.text: Weeks later, in a reconciliation
choices.why: Right, and often after the logs that would explain it are gone.

choices.text: The next time the network partitions
choices.why: It already happened; nothing about the next partition reveals it.

prompt: Why does the course run its three databases as containers rather than as packages installed on the VM?

choices.text: Because the three products are not packaged for Ubuntu, so containers are the only way to install them
choices.why: That is not the reason the section gives; the problem is many copies at once.

choices.text: Because a container is faster than a process
choices.why: A container is a process; it is not faster.

choices.text: Because up to six copies of one server must run side by side and be thrown away
choices.why: Right. One command each to start, and `docker rm -f` to put the machine back.

choices.text: Because the platform hosts the containers for you, so nothing has to be installed on your side
choices.why: The platform runs nothing; the lab is on your own computer.

prompt: You use Docker Desktop instead of the recommended VM. What does the section say to set before lesson 16?

choices.text: At least 4 GB of memory in its settings
choices.why: Right, or the three-node Cassandra cluster will not start.

choices.text: A second network for Cassandra
choices.why: One network, `nosql`, serves every lesson.

choices.text: A licence for running more than one container
choices.why: No lesson needs one.

choices.text: The Linux kernel version
choices.why: Desktop's own VM supplies the kernel; memory is the limit.

prompt: What do `-e MAX_HEAP_SIZE=256M -e HEAP_NEWSIZE=64M` change in the Cassandra container?

choices.text: They cap the disk space Cassandra may use for its data files and its commit log
choices.why: They are about memory, not disk.

choices.text: They stop Cassandra from sizing its heap from the whole machine's memory
choices.why: Right. Without them three nodes do not fit in 4 GB; with them `nodetool info` reported a 256 MB heap.

choices.text: They make Cassandra start faster by skipping the memory checks it runs at boot
choices.why: A small heap does not speed start-up; the lab still took about a minute.

choices.text: They choose which Java version runs Cassandra
choices.why: The image fixes the Java version; these set memory.

prompt: With all three servers idle, `docker stats` showed Cassandra at 595 MiB, Redis at 9.523 MiB and MongoDB at 204.1 MiB. About how many MiB is that in total? Round to the nearest ten.
After `docker rm -f mongo` and a new `docker run` with the same name, `countDocuments()` answered 0. Why?

choices.text: The new container starts with empty storage of its own
choices.why: Right. The data belonged to the container that was removed; a name is not a place.

choices.text: MongoDB deletes collections on shutdown
choices.why: After `docker stop` and `docker start` the same count answered 1.

choices.text: The `lab` collection was never written to disk
choices.why: It survived a stop and a start, so it was on disk.

choices.text: `countDocuments` counts only documents written since the server started
choices.why: It counts what the collection holds.

prompt: Why does the lab put the containers on a network called `nosql` instead of Docker's default one?

choices.text: So that containers reach each other by name
choices.why: Right. Lesson 9's three servers find each other as `mongo1`, `mongo2` and `mongo3`.

choices.text: So that the servers can be reached from the internet
choices.why: No port is published at all.

choices.text: So that traffic between them is encrypted
choices.why: A user-defined network does not encrypt anything.

choices.text: So that each container gets more memory
choices.why: Networks have nothing to do with memory.

prompt: `docker run --network nosql-lab …` printed a long id and then `network nosql-lab not found`. You fix the typo and run the line again. What happens?
hint: What did the long id mean?

choices.text: It works, since the first attempt failed
choices.why: The first attempt created a container; only starting it failed.

choices.text: A name conflict, because a container in state `Created` holds the name
choices.why: Right. `docker rm` it first.

choices.text: Docker pulls the image again and then starts the container on the correct network
choices.why: The image is already there; the name is the problem.

choices.text: The network is created automatically this time, because Docker remembers the name you asked for
choices.why: `docker run` never creates a network; `docker network create` does.

prompt: A Cassandra container shows `Exited (137)` and `OOMKilled` is `true`, on a 4 GB VM with no memory cap. Which fix addresses the cause the section names?

choices.text: Run it again until it starts
choices.why: The kernel will kill it again for the same reason.

choices.text: Publish port 9042 so that `cqlsh` can reach the node from outside the container
choices.why: A port does not change how much memory the process takes.

choices.text: Check the two `-e` heap settings and stop the containers you are not using
choices.why: Right. Without them Cassandra sizes its heap for the whole machine.

choices.text: Pull `cassandra:5.0` again, since an image that exits with 137 was damaged on download
choices.why: Exit 137 with OOMKilled is the kernel, not a damaged image.

prompt: Every `docker` command answers `permission denied while trying to connect to the docker API`. The fix is to be in the ___ group and open a new shell.
Put the lab's first build in order.
items: Create the VM and open a shell in it
Install Docker Engine and join the `docker` group
Start the three containers on it
trap: A container cannot join a network that does not exist yet.

prompt: Which of these are true of the course's three databases out of the box? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `cqlsh` reads and writes at consistency level `ONE`
choices.why: Right; lesson 17 changes it per statement.

choices.text: A Redis primary waits for its replicas before answering
choices.why: It answers at once and replicates in the background.

choices.text: A MongoDB replica set acknowledges a write once a majority has it
choices.why: Right: the implicit default.

choices.text: Each product is fixed as CP or AP and cannot be changed
choices.why: All three let you choose; the letters describe a setting.
